title: The pawn: moves and captures are different
outcomes: Taps every square a pawn can move to, including the two-square start and the diagonal captures
Knows a pawn cannot capture straight ahead and is blocked by any piece in front of it
Says in one sentence how a pawn's walk and its capture differ

steps.text: The **pawn** walks straight forward, toward the opponent's side: up the board for White, down for Black. It moves one square at a time and never backward. From its starting square it may jump two squares, but only if both squares in front are empty. Watch it on the next boards.

steps.caption: On its first move a pawn may step one square or jump two. After that it moves one square at a time.

line.say: From its starting square the pawn may jump two squares in one move.
Black makes a waiting move with the king.
Now it has moved, so it can only step one square.

steps.caption: Black's pawns walk the other way, down the board. This pawn starts on e7 and may step or jump, just like White's.

line.say: The black pawn jumps two squares from its starting square, moving down the board.
White makes a waiting move with the king.
Now it has moved, so it steps one square, still downward.

steps.caption: A black knight stands on e4. The jump is blocked, but the single step to e3 still works.

line.say: The one-square step is allowed because e3 is empty.

steps.text: A pawn **captures** differently from the way it walks: one square **diagonally forward** onto an enemy piece (one rare exception, en passant, comes later). It never captures the piece straight in front of it, so that piece simply blocks it.

steps.caption: The pawn can walk to e5 or capture the knight on d5 or the rook on f5. Capturing sets it on a new file.

line.say: The pawn captures the knight, moving one square diagonally forward.
Black moves the king; the knight is gone for good.

steps.caption: A knight stands straight in front of the pawn. The pawn cannot capture it and cannot go around, so it cannot move.

steps.prompt: Say it back. Explain to a friend why a pawn on e4 cannot take a knight on e5 but can take one on d5. Write two sentences, then compare with the model answer.

steps.text: **Model answer.** A pawn walks straight and captures diagonally forward. A piece directly in front blocks it instead of being a target; a piece on a forward diagonal can be taken. Three questions decide its moves: has it moved yet, is the square ahead empty, is an enemy on a forward diagonal? Promotion and en passant come in their own lessons.

steps.prompt: For a pawn on e4, which of the three questions decides whether it can capture: has it moved yet, is the square ahead empty, or is an enemy on a forward diagonal? Then: not yet, mostly, or ready to use it?
